rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God taught Muhammad to put His beautiful names before every action, establishing a practice for people opening speech, letters, books, and requests.
rows.anchor: أدب نبيه محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم بتعليمه تقديم ذكر أسمائه الحسنى أمام جميع أفعاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bāʾ requires a governing verb omitted from the wording; the listener recovers it from the immediately accompanying action or speech.
rows.anchor: مقتضية فعلا يكون لها جالبا، ولا فعل معها ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Qurʾān recitation the implicit verb is read, while in other acts it is rise, sit, or the relevant action, all begun with God’s name.
rows.anchor: أراد بقيله {بسم الله} [الفاتحة: 1] : أقوم بسم الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel first taught seeking refuge and then instructed Muhammad to read, rise, and sit in remembrance of his Lord.
rows.anchor: يا محمد يقول: اقرأ بذكر الله ربك، وقم واقعد بذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means beginning by naming and remembering God, rather than claiming that the act itself is performed through God’s power.
rows.anchor: أبدأ بتسمية الله وذكره قبل كل شيء، أو أقرأ بتسمية الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can use a verbal noun in a form normally associated with a noun; thus bismillah can express beginning with the act of naming.
rows.anchor: العرب قد تخرج المصادر مبهمة على أسماء مختلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic usage confirms verbal nouns can take other noun forms: ʿaṭāʾika means iʿṭāʾika, ṭūl means iṭāla, and muṣāb means iṣāba.
rows.anchor: أكفرا بعد رد الموت عني … وبعد عطائك المائة الرتاعا يريد: إعطائك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accordingly, the name stands for naming: the phrase means that one begins an action or recitation by naming God.
rows.anchor: فجعل الاسم مكان التسمية، كما جعل الكلام مكان التكليم، والعطاء مكان الإعطاء

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel’s instruction that Muhammad read and undertake actions in remembrance of God his Lord.
rows.anchor: يا محمد اقرأ بذكر الله ربك، وقم واقعد بذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī adopts the interpretation that recitation starts with God’s naming and remembrance, using His beautiful names and exalted attributes.
rows.anchor: أقرأ بتسمية الله وذكره، وأفتتح القراءة بتسمية الله، بأسمائه الحسنى، وصفاته العلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording does not mean simply “by God”; the consensus on slaughter treats saying bi-llāh without bismillah as omitting the prescribed invocation.
rows.anchor: أن قائلا لو قال عند تذكيته بعض بهائم الأنعام: بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present question concerns whether the attached “name” is a noun or a verbal noun meaning naming; the broader identity of name and named is outside this discussion.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا الموضع من مواضع الإكثار في الإبانة عن الاسم، أهو المسمى أم غيره أم هو صفة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī rejects taking Labīd’s “name of peace” simply as “peace”; that reading would license impossible Arabic such as eating the name of honey.
rows.anchor: وفي إجماع جميع العرب على إحالة ذلك ما ينبئ عن فساد تأويل من تأول قول لبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading makes al-Salām a divine name: “adhere to God’s name” after a year, with the command for adherence delayed in the wording; Ṭabarī finds this likelier.
rows.anchor: أن السلام اسم من أسماء الله؛ فجائز أن يكون لبيد عنى بقوله: ثم اسم السلام عليكما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second possible reading is a protective invocation: may God’s name be upon the two addressed people against harm.
rows.anchor: ثم تسميتي الله عليكما، كما يقول القائل للشيء يراه فيعجبه: واسم الله عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Of the two defensible readings of Labīd, the first—taking al-Salām as God’s name and an exhortation to keep His remembrance—is more apt.
rows.anchor: وكأن الوجه الأول أشبه المعنيين بقول لبيد

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says Jesus explained the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as God’s beauty, splendor, and dominion when a teacher asked about bism.
rows.anchor: فقال عيسى: الباء: بهاء الله، والسين: سناؤه، والميم: مملكته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī suspects a transmitter mistakenly joined the beginner’s alphabet letters b-s-m into bism; the explanation is impossible in ordinary Arabic when the whole basmala is recited.
rows.anchor: فأخشى أن يكون غلطا من المحدث

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines God as the one whom everything worships and every creature serves.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عباس، قال: «الله ذو الألوهية والمعبودية على خلقه أجمعين»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed derivation of Allāh from ilāh is an inference rather than an attested form heard directly from Arab speech.
rows.anchor: أما سماعا من العرب فلا، ولكن استدلالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab usage of taʾallaha for worship and seeking God supports the root’s devotional sense; a line by Ruʾba uses taʾalluhī in that sense.
rows.anchor: سبحن واسترجعن من تألهي يعني: من تعبدي وطلبي الله بعمل

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the Pharaoh passage’s ilāhataka as worship, explaining that Pharaoh worshipped rather than being worshipped.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قرأ: (ويذرك وإلاهتك) قال: عبادتك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid likewise glosses ilāhataka in the Pharaoh passage as worship, a reading also attributed there to Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، قوله: (ويذرك وإلاهتك) قال: «وعبادتك»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These explanations establish that alaha means worship and ilāha is its verbal noun, supporting the interpretation of God as the worshipped one.
rows.anchor: أن أله: عبد، وأن الإلاهة مصدره

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: A prophetic report quotes Jesus telling his teacher that Allāh is the god of gods.
rows.anchor: إن عيسى أسلمته أمه إلى الكتاب ليعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī proposes that Allāh derives from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped and the adjacent lām sounds assimilate into one doubled lām.
rows.anchor: فكذلك الله، أصله الإله، أسقطت الهمزة، التي هي فاء الاسم، فالتقت اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contraction is comparable to the Qurʾānic form lakinnā from wa-lākin anā, illustrated by a poet’s similar elision and assimilation.
rows.anchor: فكذلك الله، أصله الإله، أسقطت الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān follows the faʿlān pattern from raḥima, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, a praise form that can occur despite the root’s vowel pattern.
rows.anchor: أما الرحمن، فهو فعلان، من رحم، والرحيم فعيل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, the more distant a praise name is from its ordinary verbal pattern, the stronger its commendation; thus al-Raḥmān adds intensity beyond al-Raḥīm.
rows.anchor: أن قول القائل الرحمن عن أبنية الأسماء من فعل يفعل أشد عدولا من قوله الرحيم

rows.speaker: العرزمي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzramī distinguishes al-Raḥmān as mercy extending to all creation and al-Raḥīm as mercy toward believers.
rows.anchor: الرحمن بجميع الخلق. الرحيم قال: بالمؤمنين

rows.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet quotes Jesus distinguishing al-Raḥmān as merciful in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as merciful in the next.
rows.anchor: إن عيسى ابن مريم قال: الرحمن: رحمن الآخرة والدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī reconciles both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes universal mercy and al-Raḥīm particular mercy, whether in this life, the next, or both.
rows.anchor: ربنا جل ثناؤه رحمن جميع خلقه في الدنيا والآخرة. ورحيم المؤمنين خاصة في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain, crops, bodily and intellectual health, and other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers.
rows.anchor: في البسط في الرزق، وتسخير السحاب بالغيث، وإخراج النبات من الأرض، وصحة الأجسام والعقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the afterlife God’s universal mercy includes just treatment of everyone without the slightest wrong, while special mercy reserves guidance and the promised Garden for believers.
rows.anchor: تسويته بين جميعهم جل ذكره في عدله وقضائه، فلا يظلم أحدا منهم مثقال ذرة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to chastise; al-Raḥīm is the gentle toward those shown mercy.
rows.anchor: الرقيق الرفيق بمن أحب أن يرحمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī finds the prophetic report and al-ʿAzramī’s distinction more apt than Ibn ʿAbbās’s wording, while agreeing the names carry distinguishable meanings.
rows.anchor: والقول الذي رويناه في تأويل ذلك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وذكرناه عن العرزمي، أشبه بتأويله

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says al-Raḥmān was an exclusive divine name, then was separated from God’s name when Musaylima appropriated it.
rows.anchor: فلما اختزل الرحمن من اسمه كان الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī explains that adding al-Raḥīm distinguishes God from Musaylima: no one else has ever combined al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as names.
rows.anchor: فأما رحمن رحيم، فلم يجتمعا قط لأحد سواه، ولا يجمعان لأحد غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the claim that Arabs did not know al-Raḥmān: their question in the Qurʾān can be denial despite knowledge, as with people who recognized but rejected Muhammad.
rows.anchor: كأنه كان محالا عنده أن ينكر أهل الشرك ما كانوا عالمين بصحته

rows.speaker: سلامة بن جندل الطهوي
rows.claim: A pre-Islamic poem invokes al-Raḥmān as Lord, further demonstrating the name was familiar in Arabic.
rows.anchor: ألا ضربت تلك الفتاة هجينها … ألا قضب الرحمن ربي يمينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
rows.anchor: أن ذا الرحمة هو الذي ثبت أن له الرحمة وصح أنها له صفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
rows.anchor: أن يقدموا اسمه، ثم يتبعوه صفاته ونعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن ذا الرحمة هو الذي ثبت أن له الرحمة وصح أنها له صفة، وأن الراحم هو الموصوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
rows.anchor: أن يقدموا اسمه، ثم يتبعوه صفاته ونعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī explains that God’s unique name remains exclusive even if people bear names such as Saʿīd while being its opposite.
rows.anchor: وإن قصد المتسمي به ما يقصد المتسمي بسعيد وهو شقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī places Allāh first because no other being shares divine worship, then al-Raḥmān, which is also reserved for God, before the shared descriptor al-Raḥīm.
rows.anchor: فبدأ الله جل ذكره باسمه الذي هو الله؛ لأن الألوهية ليست لغيره جل ثناؤه بوجه من الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāh and al-Raḥmān are reserved for God, while al-Raḥīm may describe creatures; no one shares God’s divinity or deserves His exclusive names.
rows.anchor: قد يجوز وصف كثير ممن هو دون الله من خلقه ببعض صفات الرحمة

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī calls al-Raḥmān a forbidden name for others; Ṭabarī says the community’s consensus already establishes the prohibition.
rows.anchor: حدثنا محمد بن بشار، قال: حدثنا حماد بن مسعدة، عن عوف، عن الحسن، قال: «الرحمن اسم ممنوع»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamd lillāh is gratitude and praise owed exclusively to God for countless blessings, including capacity for worship, provision, and guidance to lasting bliss.
rows.anchor: دنياهم من الرزق وغذاهم به من نعيم العيش

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains praise as gratitude, submission to God, and acknowledging His blessings, guidance, and originating gifts.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله: هو الشكر، والاستخذاء لله، والإقرار بنعمته وهدايته وابتدائه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says that saying “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude for which God gives an increase.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إذا قلت الحمد لله رب العالمين، فقد شكرت الله فزادك»

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār calls al-ḥamd praise of God; the narration does not specify whether he means praise for names and attributes or for blessings.
rows.anchor: من قال الحمد لله فذلك ثناء على الله

rows.speaker: الأسود بن سريع
rows.claim: A prophetic report says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, and that He praised Himself with “Praise belongs to God.”
rows.anchor: ليس شيء أحب إليه الحمد من الله تعالى، ولذلك أثنى على نفسه فقال: الحمد لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic allows praise and thanks to overlap: the phrase “praise belongs to God, in thanks” works because each term can occupy the other’s place.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله شكرا بالصحة. فقد تبين إذ كان ذلك عند جميعهم صحيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article makes al-ḥamd signify all praise and complete gratitude belong to God; without it the wording would describe only this speaker’s praise.
rows.anchor: أن دخولهما في الحمد منبئ على أن معناه: جميع المحامد والشكر الكامل لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inherited nominative reading al-ḥamdu preserves the intended universal claim; deliberately reading it accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment.
rows.anchor: تتابعت قراءة القراء وعلماء الأمة على رفع الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whole passage is God’s speech: He first praises Himself, then teaches and obliges worshippers to say both the praise and “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: فقال لهم: قولوا: الحمد لله رب العالمين وقولوا: إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic regularly omits words recoverable from context, as in poetic answers and farewell formulas; a known meaning makes the unspoken expression unnecessary.
rows.anchor: فكذلك ما حذف من قول الله تعالى ذكره: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2]

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that Gabriel told Muhammad to say the praise confirms Ṭabarī’s implied command interpretation.
rows.anchor: أن جبريل قال لمحمد: قل يا محمد: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can mean an obeyed master; Labīd and al-Nābigha use it for the lords of Kindah and the speaker’s patron.
rows.anchor: فالسيد المطاع فيها يدعى ربا، ومن ذلك قول لبيد بن ربيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can mean one who repairs or sets something right; al-Farazdaq’s unrepaired hide and ʿAlqama’s neglected affairs illustrate this sense.
rows.anchor: والرجل المصلح للشيء يدعى ربا. ومنه قول الفرزدق بن غالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can also mean owner; these lexical senses converge in God as incomparable sovereign, caretaker of creation, and possessor of command.
rows.anchor: فربنا جل ثناؤه السيد الذي لا شبه له، ولا مثل في سؤدده، والمصلح أمر خلقه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Lord owns all creation—heavens, earths, their inhabitants, and what lies between—known and unknown, and resembles nothing.
rows.anchor: يقول قل الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله، السموات كلهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀlamīn is a plural collective with no singular of the same form; ʿālam denotes a class of peoples, and each species or generation is its own world.
rows.anchor: من كل صنف منها عالم ذلك القرن وذلك الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet al-ʿAjjāj calls his own generation “this world,” illustrating how a time’s people form a distinct ʿālam.
rows.anchor: فخندف هامة هذا العالم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes the worlds as all creation: the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and what is known or unknown.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك، عن ابن عباس: " {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Other reports from Ibn ʿAbbās define the worlds as jinn and humans; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid report the same narrower gloss.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة، عن ابن عباس: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] : الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the worlds are jinn and humans, with a related report explaining each human and jinn community as a world of its own.
rows.anchor: ابن آدم، والجن والإنس كل أمة منهم عالم على حدته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid also interprets “Lord of the worlds” as referring to humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد: " {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: الإنس والجن

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses the worlds as every distinct class or kind.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: كل صنف: عالم

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says humans and jinn are worlds, alongside either fourteen or eighteen thousand angelic worlds on earth, created to worship; he is uncertain which count.
rows.anchor: الإنس عالم، والجن عالم، وما سوى ذلك ثمانية عشر ألف عالم، أو أربعة عشر ألف عالم

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj gives the worlds as jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، في قوله: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī argues the basmala is not a verse of the Opening: otherwise al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm would repeat immediately, word for word and sense for sense, without an intervening divider.
rows.anchor: لو كان ذلك كذلك لكان ذلك إعادة آية بمعنى واحد ولفظ واحد مرتين من غير فصل

rows.speaker: جماعة من أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك من المؤخر الذي معناه التقديم، وإنما هو: الحمد لله الرحمن الرحيم رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry by Jarīr and Qurʾān 18:2 illustrate fronting and delaying in Arabic; the apparent order can place the “upright” description before its intended antecedent.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي أنزل على عبده الكتاب قيما ولم يجعل له عوجا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reorderings support the interpreters who deny that the basmala belongs to the Opening as a verse.
rows.anchor: دليل شاهد على صحة قول من أنكر أن تكون {بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم} [الفاتحة: 1] من فاتحة الكتاب آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī says he already detailed the transmitted reading variants and his preferred reading in his book of readings; this treatise focuses on interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقد استقصينا حكاية الرواية عمن روي عنه في ذلك قراءة في كتاب القراءات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the “king” reading, God alone possesses kingship on Judgment Day, when earthly tyrants become humbled and powerless.
rows.anchor: أن لله الملك يوم الدين خالصا دون جميع خلقه الذين كانوا قبل ذلك في الدنيا ملوكا جبابرة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the owner reading as no one having authority over judgment that day as they did in worldly life; he cites limits on speech and intercession.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك، عن عبد الله بن عباس: {مالك يوم الدين} يقول: " لا يملك أحد في ذلك اليوم معه حكما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī prefers the “king” reading: every king is an owner, but an owner need not be king, so kingship affirms a greater and more exclusive quality.
rows.anchor: أن لا ملك إلا وهو مالك، وقد يكون المالك لا ملكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because “Lord of the worlds” already says God owns and governs all creation, “king of Judgment Day” adds information instead of repeating ownership.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان جل ذكره قد أنبأهم عن ملكه إياهم كذلك بقوله: {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī rejects limiting “Lord of the worlds” to earthly creation or Muhammad’s own era: the text supplies no such limit, and the Qurʾān distinguishes worlds across successive communities.
rows.anchor: أن قوله: {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] محصور معناه على الخبر عن ربوبية عالم الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾān 45:16 and 3:110 show that Israel’s earlier age and Muhammad’s community are distinct worlds; believers in Muhammad’s message are best from his age onward.
rows.anchor: قد فضل أمة نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم على سائر الأمم الخالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that mālik means the one who brings about Judgment Day does not distinguish a new domain: resurrection restores the same people already included among the worlds.
rows.anchor: إقامة القيامة إنما هي إعادة الخلق الذين قد بادوا لهيئاتهم التي كانوا عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative mālika can be construed as a vocative, “O Owner of Judgment Day,” to connect with the following direct address “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: كأنه أراد: يا مالك يوم الدين، إياك نعبد، وإياك نستعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabarī says the accusative is unnecessary: revelation commands Muhammad to say both the descriptions of God and then the direct address, and Arabic allows this shift within reported speech.
rows.anchor: قل أيضا يا محمد: {إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين} [الفاتحة: 5]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry by Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī and Labīd, and Qurʾān 10:22, show that Arabic can move from third-person report to direct address without requiring a vocative construction.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا كنتم في الفلك وجرين بهم بريح طيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative reading of mālik is impermissible because the recognized readers and scholars unanimously reject it.
rows.anchor: فقراءة: {مالك يوم الدين} محظورة غير جائزة
